title: Robots That Admit 'I'm Not Sure' Are the Future of AI
summary: Picture a robot arm on a factory floor. It's been trained to assemble smartphones, but suddenly a new component with a slightly different shape arrives. A traditional robot might either freeze or smash it—costly mistakes. Yen-Ling Kuo, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Virginia, is solving this with a technique called Diff-DAgger, which earned her the IEEE Robotics and Automation Society's inaugural Outstanding Women in Robotics and Automation Early Career Contribution Award. The core innovation? Teaching robots to recognize and act on uncertainty. Diff-DAgger uses a diffusion policy—a generative model that predicts multiple possible actions—and estimates how confident the robot should be in each. When confidence is low, the robot can request human guidance or choose the safest option. In tests, this approach significantly improved task success rates while slashing the need for constant supervision. It's a crucial leap toward deploying complex, data-hungry models in real-world interactive robot learning. Kuo's path to this breakthrough was fueled by a lifelong curiosity about how things work. Growing up in Taiwan, she was inspired by Michael Faraday's story and learned programming logic through Logo, a child-friendly language with a turtle cursor. Later, at Google, she worked on the Shop the Look initiative, linking natural language descriptions to product images—a project that forced her to confront the black-box nature of neural networks. "I was applying the neural network tools," she recalls, "but I didn't have 100 percent certainty about how they actually worked." That discomfort planted the seed for her current research. Now, Kuo's work promises to make robots more adaptable in unpredictable settings, from disaster response to home assistance. By letting machines say "I'm not sure," she's building a future where robots are not just powerful, but also humble enough to ask for help.
why_it_matters: As robots move out of factories and into our homes, hospitals, and roads, machines that know when they are in over their head could prevent dangerous mistakes. This kind of humble AI also changes what it means to be 'intelligent'—showing that admitting doubt is not a weakness but a safety feature that builds trust between humans and machines.

background_read: Teaching machines to handle uncertainty is a major shift from the earliest days of robotics, when robots followed rigid, pre-programmed paths and broke down in new situations.

The Diff-DAgger technique builds on diffusion models—a type of AI that became famous in 2022 for creating detailed images from simple text prompts, like 'a cat wearing a spacesuit.' Yen-Ling Kuo (an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Virginia) adapted this idea so a robot imagines several possible movements instead of just one.

Kuo's curiosity was sparked as a child in Taiwan by the story of Michael Faraday, a self-taught 19th-century scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction and built the first electric motor, and by Logo, a programming language from the 1960s that let children explore logic by commanding a turtle cursor on screen.

Her early discomfort with neural networks at Google—where she worked on the Shop the Look project that matched text descriptions to product images—showed her that even experts often cannot fully explain an AI's choices. That experience planted the seed for building robots that know their own limits.

The IEEE Robotics and Automation Society, which gave Kuo its early-career award, is a global professional organization that sets standards and promotes research in robotics, from factory arms to self-driving cars.

perspectives.description: Robots that gauge their own uncertainty could dramatically reduce costly accidents in manufacturing and make robot helpers safer in unpredictable environments like disaster sites or elder care. The technique slashes the need for constant human oversight, saving time and money while making automation more reliable.

Relying on human intervention when confidence is low might slow down operations in time-critical settings. If a robot frequently asks for help, the efficiency gains of automation could be lost, and the system could still fail in truly novel situations where even a human is unsure what to do.

This work reflects a broader historical pattern in artificial intelligence: moving from brittle, overconfident expert systems toward models that acknowledge their limitations. Just as early industrial robots were locked in cages, modern AI is now being designed to collaborate by communicating uncertainty rather than acting as an unreadable black box.

The next step could involve robots that not only ask for help but gradually learn from those human corrections to handle similar situations on their own—building a lifelong learning loop. Privacy, ethics, and job displacement will become even more pressing as robots enter intimate spaces like living rooms, requiring clear rules on when a machine should stop and seek a person.
